{{More footnotes needed|date=July 2025}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Dedekind sums''' are certain finite sums of products of a [[sawtooth function]].  [[Dedekind]] introduced them in the 1880's to express the [[functional equation]] of the [[Dedekind eta function]], in a commentary to [[Bernhard Riemann]]'s collected papers.<ref name="dedekind">{{cite book |last=Dedekind |first=Richard |authorlink=Richard Dedekind |title=Collected Works of Bernhard Riemann |publisher=Dover Publ., New York |pages=466-478 |chapter=Erläuterungen zu den Fragmenten XXVIII |date=1953}}</ref>. They have subsequently been much studied in [[number theory]] but also occur in some results in [[topology]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hirzebruch |first1=Friedrich |authorlink1=Friedrich Hirzebruch |last2=Zagier |authorlink2=Don Zagier |first2=Don |date=1974 |title=The Atiyah–Singer Theorem and Elementary Number Theory |publisher=Publish or Perish |location=Boston, Mass.}}</ref>
[[geometric combinatorics]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pommersheim |first=James E. |date=1993 |title=Toric varieties, lattice points and Dedekind sums |journal=Math. Ann. |volume=295 |issue=1 |pages=1–24}}</ref>
[[algebraic geometry]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Garoufalidis |first1=Stavros |last2=Pommersheim |first2=James E. |date=2001 |title=Values of zeta functions at negative integers, Dedekind sums and toric geometry |journal=J. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=1–23}}</ref> and
[[computational complexity]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Knuth |first=Donald E. |authorlink=Donald E. Knuth |date=1981 |title=The Art of Computer Programming. Vol. 2 |location=Reading, Mass. |publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Co.}}</ref> Dedekind sums have been generalized in various directions, satisfying a large number of functional equations; this article lists only a small fraction of these.

== Definition ==
Define the [[sawtooth function]] <math>(\!( \, )\!) : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> as  
:<math>(\!(x)\!)=\begin{cases}
x-\lfloor x\rfloor - 1/2, &\mbox{if }x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z};\\
0,&\mbox{if }x\in\mathbb{Z}.
\end{cases}</math>

We then define the '''Dedekind sum'''

:<math>D: \mathbb{Z}^2\times \mathbb{Z}_{> 0} \to \mathbb{Q}</math>

by

:<math>D(a,b;c)=\sum_{n=1}^{c-1} \left(\!\!\left( \frac{an}{c} \right)\!\!\right) \! \left(\!\!\left( \frac{bn}{c} \right)\!\!\right).</math>

For the case ''a''&nbsp;=&thinsp;1, one often writes

:''s''(''b'', ''c'') = ''D''(1, ''b''; ''c'').

==Simple formulae==
Note that ''D'' is symmetric in ''a'' and ''b'', i.e.,

:<math>D(a,b;c)=D(b,a;c),</math>

and that, by the oddness of (( )),

:''D''(−''a'', ''b''; ''c'') = −''D''(''a'', ''b''; ''c'').

By the periodicity of ''D'' in its first two arguments, the third argument being the length of the period for both,

:''D''(''a'', ''b''; ''c'') = ''D''(''a''+''kc'', ''b''+''lc''; ''c''), for all integers ''k'',''l''.

If ''d'' is a positive integer, then

:''D''(''ad'', ''bd''; ''cd'') = ''dD''(''a'', ''b''; ''c''),

:''D''(''ad'', ''bd''; ''c'') = ''D''(''a'', ''b''; ''c''), if (''d'', ''c'') = 1,

:''D''(''ad'', ''b''; ''cd'') = ''D''(''a'', ''b''; ''c''), if (''d'', ''b'') = 1.

There is a proof for the last equality making use of

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{c-1} \left( \!\!\left( \frac{n+x}{c} \right) \!\!\right)= (\!( x )\!),\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}.</math>

Furthermore, ''az'' = 1 (mod ''c'') implies ''D''(''a'', ''b''; ''c'') = ''D''(1, ''bz''; ''c'').

==Alternative forms==

If ''b'' and ''c'' are [[coprime]], we may write ''s''(''b'', ''c'') as

:<math>s(b,c)=\frac{-1}{c} \sum_\omega
\frac{1} { (1-\omega^b) (1-\omega ) } 
+\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4c},</math>

where the sum extends over the ''c''-th [[roots of unity]] other than 1, i.e., over all <math>\omega</math> such that <math>\omega^c=1</math> and <math>\omega\not=1</math>.<ref name="beckrobins">{{cite book |last1=Beck |first1=Matthias |last2=Robins |first2=Sinai |date=2015 |title=Computing the Continuous Discretely: Integer-Point Enumeration in Polyhedra |location=New York |publisher=Springer |chapter=Chapter 8. Dedekind Sums |isbn=978-1-4939-2969-6}}</ref>

Equivalently, if ''b'' and ''c'' are coprime, then

:<math>s(b,c)=\frac{1}{4c}\sum_{n=1}^{c-1} 
\cot \left(\frac{\pi n}{c}\right)
\cot \left(\frac{\pi nb}{c}\right).
</math>

This reformulation mirrors the fact that the above cotangent function is the [[discrete Fourier transform]] of the sawtooth function.<ref name="beckrobins" />

==The reciprocity law==
Dedekind<ref name="dedekind" /> proved that, if ''b'' and ''c'' are coprime positive integers then

:<math>s(b,c)+s(c,b) =\frac{1}{12}\left(\frac{b}{c}+\frac{1}{bc}+\frac{c}{b}\right)-\frac{1}{4}.</math>

There exist several proofs from first principles, and Dedekind's reciprocity law is equivalent to [[quadratic reciprocity]].<ref>{{cite book | last1=Rademacher | first1=Hans | authorlink1=Hans Rademacher | last2=Grosswald | first2=Emil | authorlink2=Emil Grosswald | title=Dedekind Sums |publisher=Math. Assoc. Amer. |date=1972 |isbn=0-88385-016-8}}</ref>

Rewriting the reciprocity law as

:<math>12bc \left( s(b,c) + s(c,b) \right) = b^2 + c^2 - 3bc + 1,</math>

it follows that the number 6''c''&nbsp;''s''(''b'',''c'') is an integer.

If ''k'' = (3, ''c'') then

:<math>12bc\, s(c,b)=0 \mod kc</math>

and

:<math>12bc\, s(b,c)=b^2+1 \mod kc.</math>

A relation that is prominent in the theory of the [[Dedekind eta function]] is the following. Let ''q'' = 3, 5, 7 or 13 and let ''n'' = 24/(''q''&nbsp;−&thinsp;1). Then given integers ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' with ''ad''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''bc''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 (thus belonging to the [[modular group]]), with ''c'' chosen so that ''c''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''kq'' for some integer ''k'' &gt; 0, define
 
:<math>\delta = s(a,c) - \frac{a+d}{12c} - s(a,k) + \frac{a+d}{12k}.</math>

Then <math>n \delta</math> is an [[parity (mathematics)|even]] integer.

==Rademacher's generalization of the reciprocity law==
[[Hans Rademacher]] found the following generalization of the reciprocity law for Dedekind sums:<ref>{{cite journal | last=Rademacher | first=Hans | authorlink=Hans Rademacher | title=Generalization of the reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums | journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]] | volume=21 | pages=391–397 | year=1954 | zbl=0057.03801 | doi=10.1215/s0012-7094-54-02140-7}}</ref>  If ''a'', ''b'', and ''c'' are pairwise coprime positive integers, then

:<math>D(a,b;c)+D(b,c;a)+D(c,a;b)=\frac{1}{12}\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{abc}-\frac{1}{4}.</math>

Hence, the above triple sum vanishes [[if and only if]] (''a'', ''b'', ''c'') is a Markov triple, i.e., a solution of the [[Markov equation]]  

:<math>a^2+b^2+c^2=3abc.</math>
